I am surprised to say I am endeared by this animation style— the movie looks quite nice and preserves the signature look of the show while nicely translating its visuals to 3D. Beyond the 2004 original I have not seen any other SpongeBob films, but I have seen that original many times, and clearly so have the filmmakers behind The Search for SquarePants . Many of the visual gags from that film are referenced, remixed, or reinterpreted for this movie, which I don’t have much innate objection to when they’ve been releasing new SpongeBob films at a clip of about one every five years— just long enough of a gap that the children that tuned in for their last effort have very likely outgrown the target demographic by the next. 3–5 years has long been treated as the standard for churn when it comes to IP designed for children, so who am I to judge if a joke that worked for me as a child is reworked for the next generation? What I struggle much more to forgive is the repetition of themes. In this film, the titular ‘Bob strives to be seen as a “big guy”, which is a transparent euphemism for maturity. This echoes the sponge of 24 years prior, who wished to be seen as a man. His journey in both films includes episodes obviously inspired by The Odyssey. He is manipulated into action by a scheming green villain. He briefly travels to the surface world to interact with real-life humans. The story of SpongeBob, forever unfinished, becomes a Sisyphean nightmare about a boy incapable of ever truly growing up— after all, what responsible adult would choose to live in a pineapple?

Si me preguntan por uno de mis primeros recuerdos en una sala de cine, inevitablemente aparece la primera película de Bob Esponja. La recuerdo con un cariño inmenso, ligada a esos miércoles de cine con mi mamá donde intercambiábamos tapas de gaseosa para conseguir la entrada a mitad de precio. Por eso, mi conexión con esta cinta es, en su gran mayoría, pura y vibrante nostalgia. La película logra rescatar la esencia del humor absurdo de las primeras temporadas de la serie, ese estilo que realmente te atrapa. Bob sigue siendo ese personaje noble, ingenuo y un poco tonto que a menudo es manipulado por los demás, pero que nunca pierde su esencia. Además, el slapstick —el humor de golpes y situaciones físicas extremas— funciona a la perfección; admitámoslo: ver sufrir a Calamardo es algo que, por alguna razón, nunca deja de ser divertido. Es una película redonda para disfrutar en familia. Siempre me ha fascinado cómo integran a actores reales en este mundo submarino; esa estética que parece 'mal hecha' o intencionalmente cutre es, al mismo tiempo, lo que la hace visualmente icónica y brillante. Even after giving this another watch, while I do still like it overall, I would still consider this to be my least favorite of the four main SpongeBob movies. And I say that because, as a longtime fan of SpongeBob, it is noticeable that the story does reuse some elements from the previous films (such as SpongeBob wanting to prove that he's not just a kid, which was part of the first film's story, the climax happening on the surface like in the second film, and characters going after SpongeBob to save him, like in the third film). Additionally, the story can be a little predictable at times, since we know that SpongeBob is being tricked by the Flying Dutchman before he reveals it to him. And lastly, like I said in my first first review of this film, the film also repeats the main flaw the first film has, which is sidelining some of the main characters of the show and only focusing on a small number of them. But even with those, there are still things to like about the film. The animation is great, the voice actors give great performances, the fight scenes are good, it has a good amount of funny moments, and it is in general a good movie to watch overall. So even if I'd still say that this is one of the weaker SpongeBob movies, I still like it overall and would say it's worth watching.

If I had a nickel for every time Derek Drymon directed a fourth installment of a movie franchise known for zany and wacky shenanigans of colorful characters that had scripts that took some story elements from the first installments, I would have two nickels! Which isn't a lot, but it's weird that it happened twice, right? I, like a grand majority of people, have had this childlike, whimsical, hilarious, optimistic, loving, and hardworking sponge as a major part of my childhood and have even implemented his way of going about the world into our daily lives. I have watched from the first seasons, all the way up to season 12, and have watched all of his movies up to this point. Sponge on the Run has its genuine moments but is severely lacking in other important areas. Sponge Out of Water was a blast and a half adventure, but the first movie is genuinely one of my favorites, and I don't believe anything could top its humor, animation, story, spectacle, and characterization of these characters we have come to love. I have noticed that every movie was helmed by someone heavily involved throughout the show and its run. The legendary creator, Stephen Hillenburg, for the first movie, the showrunner for the show when Hillenburg left after the first few seasons, Paul Tibbit for SOoW, and the co-developer of the show, Tim Hill, for SOTR. Now we have come to this movie, helmed by Derek Drymon, the creative director for the show in its earlier seasons. I was cautiously optimistic, as I liked Drymon’s direction in the things I've seen, but I was wondering how exactly funny it would be, how exactly the cast would be characterized, and whether the plot could carry a whole movie. They also really wanted to emphasize how this movie would bring back vibes of the first iconic seasons. So they intentionally were trying to raise expectations. How did I like it? I honestly had a blast, just as much as I had with Sponge Out of Water, if I am being totally honest. If I wasn’t laughing at how surprisingly funny and zany it could get with well-timed jokes and slapstick, I was always smiling from ear to ear. I even enjoyed the plot and the story, where the BOB wants to be seen as a BIG GUY and be respected as such by being brave, especially by Mr. Krabs, one of the biggest guys he knows, so he goes along with Patrick to help the Flying Dutchman to the Underworld to prove he is indeed a BIG GUY, who was surprisingly well-acted by Mark Hamill. Not only was the comedy on point for me, but also, I really enjoyed the relationships displayed in this movie, especially the father-son dynamic with Krabs and SpongeBob. Even has a nice enough message, though I do admit it is taking a lot from the first movie and is not as well executed as it was then. The animation, while not as detailed as SOTR, is stylised in a way where it is essentially how the show looks in 3D. While this is not a perfect movie, let alone a perfect SpongeBob movie, I still had a lot of fun and even felt as happy to see SpongeBob on the big screen through this movie as I was when I was a kid rewatching the first filam an the constant reruns of episodes. So in a sense, I do feel it somewhat captured the vibes of the early seasons, just a bit. Well done, Drymon!
